questions.explanation: The liver normally clears bilirubin, the yellow pigment left over when old red blood cells are broken down. When hepatitis inflames the liver, bilirubin backs up into the blood, settles into the skin and the whites of the eyes as jaundice, and the excess leaving through the kidneys darkens the urine — one backup explaining both findings. Myoglobin can also darken urine, but it comes from crushed or damaged muscle, and this patient's picture is an inflamed liver, not a muscle injury.

choices: Both medics' stress systems switched on; the one who recovered is the one whose arousal later settled back to baseline — that capacity to bounce back after activation is resilience.

questions.explanation: Resilience is not the absence of a stress reaction — both medics' alarms fired that night, exactly as they should. It is the recovery half of the cycle: stress hormones and arousal rise for the event and then settle back to baseline. Avoidance is actually a risk pattern for lasting symptoms, not a recovery strategy, and the whole response is driven by the body's stress chemistry — the HPA axis and the adrenaline system — not by deciding to be tough.

questions.explanation: Critical incident stress management is a system, not a session, and its pieces are timed on purpose: a defusing within hours, a structured debriefing about 24 to 72 hours later, then follow-up. Working through the event early with trained peers helps responders process it and normalizes the stress reaction, and the follow-up pieces spot the few who need professional help — which the program refers out for, never replaces. No single session, including the debriefing, prevents PTSD by itself.

choices: OSHA writes workplace safety standards that carry the force of law, so it can inspect a workplace and cite and fine the employer; CDC publishes infection-control guidance and recommendations but has no power to enforce them.

questions.explanation: A citation with a fine means a legal standard was violated — that is OSHA's enforcement role, and the written exposure control plan requirement sits in OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). CDC's infection-control guidance shapes what a good plan contains, but guidance is advice: CDC cannot inspect your station, cite your service, or fine it. Only OSHA does that, because its standards are law and CDC's publications are recommendations.

choices: He cannot decline at all; the standard requires every EMT with exposure risk to complete the vaccine series.

questions.explanation: Under OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030), the vaccine is the employer's standing duty, not a one-time offer: it must be offered free, after training and within 10 working days of assignment to duties with exposure risk. An employee who declines signs a declination form so the refusal is documented — but the door stays open, and if he asks later while still exposed, the employer must offer the series free again. The standard requires the offer; it cannot force the vaccination itself.

choices: Clinicians report cases to their state health department; states share their data with CDC; CDC coordinates laboratory testing and outbreak specialists and issues national guidance.
